head: byoa docs
text: byoa, short for "bring your own agent", is the simplest way to let your users bring their own AI subscription to power the agents in your app.

head: The future of AI-native apps
text: AI-native apps are the future. But an app that buys its AI at API prices must pass that cost on to its users. So it must choose: a frontier model, and a high price for each user, or a cheap model, and a worse agent. AI subscriptions solve this. We bet on a future where everyone has a $20 AI plan, or the same in another form, and that plan powers every app they use. In that future, every app is AI-native, so nobody says "AI-native app" anymore. AI is like electricity, and an AI subscription is like a portable battery pack. Battery packs come in different sizes, and one pack powers all the appliances in your home. This is the economy we bet on. We build byoa to make it come sooner, so that every developer can build on it. Diagram: Where the power comes from and who pays for it. Today: the AI labs sell tokens to each app through its API key, and each app, such as a notes app, a mail app and your app, pays per token and puts that cost in its price. With byoa: each user owns one battery, their own AI plan, and it plugs into every app they use. Your app passes on only the cost of the sandbox.

head: What byoa does
text: Each user powers the agent features of your app with their own AI subscription: they sign in to it one time. Today byoa supports Claude (in Claude Code), ChatGPT (in Codex), Grok (in Grok Build) and OpenCode Go (beta), and more are coming soon. When your app has work for the AI, byoa runs that user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build in a sandbox, with the user's tools, and streams the result back. The user's plan pays for the AI. Your app pays only for the sandbox. Diagram: Who brings what. Your app brings the product, the sandbox account, and one call: agents.run. Each user brings their AI plan, such as Claude, ChatGPT or Grok, and their tools, such as Notion or Gmail. byoa puts them together in a new sandbox for each job: it runs the user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build with their tools, and streams the result back to your app. The user's plan pays for the AI. Your app pays only for the sandbox. byoa is an open-source library (Apache 2.0). It runs inside your app's own backend. It is not a hosted service. Start with Getting started. To learn the parts first, read the Overview. To see which plans work, read Supported AI subscriptions.

head: Why and when you need byoa
text: You want your app to have an AI agent that does real work for each user: it reads and changes the user's data, calls the user's tools, and writes files. To build this yourself, you need many parts: - an agent loop as good as Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build, and its updates; - a sandbox for each user, which starts, pauses and ends at the right times; - a sign-in to each user's AI plan, and safe storage of that login; - an OAuth connection to each of the user's MCP tools, with the tokens kept out of the agent's reach. And with your own API key, your app buys every token at API prices, and your users pay for them in your price. byoa gives you all of these parts as one library, and the user's own plan pays for the AI. Diagram: Your backend, before and after. Build it yourself: your app, an agent loop, sandbox control, AI sign-in and login storage, and MCP OAuth and token storage, and an AI bill per token, at API prices. With byoa: your app and byoa, one npm install, and no AI bill, because the user's plan pays. Use byoa when: - your users already pay for Claude, ChatGPT, Grok or OpenCode Go, and you do not want to pay for their AI or sell them AI credits; - your app's AI work is agent work, with many steps, tools and files, not one chat answer; - you want Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build as your agent, not a loop of your own; - you want each user's tools, such as Notion or Gmail, in each job, after one connection. head: How byoa works
text: Your app brings the product. Each user brings the agent. You build the app and pick the sandbox. Each user brings their plan and their tools. byoa runs inside your backend and runs each job in that user's own sandbox. Think of the user's AI subscription as a battery pack, and of your app as an appliance. The user brings the battery. byoa is the plug: it connects the user's plan, and the user's tools, to the agent features of your app. Your app supplies only the place where the agent runs, the sandbox.

head: Who brings what
text: Diagram: You build the app and import byoa. You pay only for the sandbox. Each user signs in with their own Claude, ChatGPT or Grok plan, which pays for the AI, and connects their tools once. Your app code calls agents.run. byoa is a library inside your app's backend, and keeps AI logins and MCP grants in your database. Below your backend's edge, byoa drives three things that run outside it: a new sandbox for each job at E2B, Daytona, Instabox or Sprites on your account, where the user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build runs; the AI labs, whose model calls the user's own plan pays; and the user's MCP servers, which get the real token from byoa's proxy. - You, the developer, build the app, pick the sandbox provider (E2B, Daytona, Instabox or Sprites, on your own account) and own the database. You import byoa into your app's backend. - The end user uses your app. They have a Claude, ChatGPT or Grok plan, and accounts in tools such as Notion or Gmail. They sign in on the lab's own page one time, and connect each MCP tool one time. - byoa is a library in your backend. It keeps the user's AI login and MCP grants in your database, encrypted with your key. For each job, it gets a sandbox at your provider and runs the user's own, unmodified Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build there. - The AI labs (Anthropic, OpenAI) get the model calls. The user's own plan pays for them, not your API bill. - The MCP servers get the real token from byoa's proxy in your backend, never from the sandbox

head: The problem
text: To make an app AI-native, you run a big lab's harness (Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build) in a sandbox, with the user's own AI plan. For each app, you must build the same connection layer again: - the user's AI login, through the real CLI; - the user's MCP connections and their OAuth tokens, with one refresh owner; - the user's skills and AGENTS.md; - the harness install and its updates; - the code that connects all of this to one sandbox provider. byoa is that layer, as a library, so you do not build it again for each app.

head: What byoa is, and what it is not
text: - byoa is a library. It runs inside your app's own backend (Node, Bun or Convex). Cloudflare Workers support is planned. - byoa stores tokens in your own database, through a store adapter. - byoa is not a hosted service. We do not run a server, and we never see your users' tokens. Version 1 Later --------- Agents Claude Code, Codex, Grok Build Gemini or Antigravity, maybe User plans Claude, ChatGPT, Grok, OpenCode Go key (beta) Sandboxes E2B, Daytona, Instabox, Sprites (Fly.io) other providers Backends Node, Convex actions Cloudflare Workers Token stores Convex, Postgres, or your own with get, put, delete and compare-and-set

head: How a job runs
text: Your app calls agents.run(userId, task). byoa takes the user's sandbox, loads the user's setup, and runs the user's own harness on the user's own plan. The sandbox lifecycle has every step and every decision. Diagram: One job, from agents.run to the end event 1. Your app calls agents.run. agents.run(userId, { harness, task, mcp, setup }). 2. Take the user's sandbox. By default, resume the user's kept sandbox (a conversation has one of its own), or create it for the first job. With sandboxPer 'job', create a new one. 3. Load the setup. The pinned harness, the skills, AGENTS.md, and an MCP config that points to your proxy with a job token. 4. Copy the AI login in. From your database, decrypted in your backend. Login files: login files in. 5. Run the harness. Text, tool calls and permission requests stream back as events. MCP calls go through the proxy. 6. close() This is the end. End the job token, save the login back if the CLI changed it, remove it from the sandbox, then pause or destroy the sandbox. Login files: files removed. The user's AI login and MCP grants stay in your database between jobs. A kept sandbox keeps the files that the app wrote there and the installed harness, but no login. A job of a conversation also continues the harness's session of the earlier jobs, and keeps the job folder (what carries over).

head: Real tokens never go into the sandbox
text: The agent in the sandbox gets a short-lived job token, for one job and one user. The proxy in your backend adds the real MCP token to each request. Diagram: How an MCP call from the sandbox gets the real token 1. The harness calls an MCP tool. Its MCP config points to your proxy, at <proxyUrl>/<name>, with the job token. It has no real MCP token. 2. Question: Is the job token good for this server? If yes: go on to step 3. - If no: Refuse the call. This is the end. The job ended, or the job did not get this server. 3. Add the real token. From your database, encrypted with your key. byoa refreshes it when it is due, with one refresh owner. 4. Send the request on to the MCP server. This is the end. The answer goes back to the harness. The real token does not. MCP tools and the proxy has the details, and AI login says where the user's AI login is at each step.

head: Getting started
text: New to byoa? Read the Introduction first. In short: byoa is a library in your app's backend. Each user signs in to their own Claude, ChatGPT or Grok plan one time, and connects each MCP tool one time. When your app has work for the AI, byoa runs that user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build in a sandbox, with the user's tools, and streams the events back to your app. The user's plan pays for the AI, and your app pays for the sandbox. This page takes you from npm install to a first agent job: one agents object, two routes, a sign-in and a job. A new app needs fewer than 50 lines of its own code for this. The to-do example, a chat with the agent, uses byoa in 49.

head: Install
text: Install byoa from npm. Its package is @madeyexz/byoa, because npm does not allow the name byoa: Also install the sandbox SDK that your app uses: e2b for E2B, @daytona/sdk for Daytona. Instabox, Sprites and the local sandbox need none. byoa needs Node 22.18 or later, or Bun. To use the newest commit on main before it is released, install from GitHub: npm install github:madeyexz/byoa.

head: Get a sandbox API key
text: Your app pays for the sandboxes, so your app needs its own account and API key at one sandbox provider. Make an account, make a key, and put the key in your backend's environment. Do not send the key to the browser. - E2B: sign up, then copy a key from API keys. byoa reads E2B_API_KEY. The free plan gives $100 of credit one time and runs 10 sandboxes at a time; a paused sandbox does not count. A sandbox runs for 1 hour at most before it must pause, so one job can take at most 1 hour (billing and limits). - Daytona: sign up, then make a key in API keys. byoa reads DAYTONA_API_KEY. A new account gets $200 of compute (pricing). On Tier 1 and 2, a sandbox can reach only allowed domains. - Instabox: sign up, then make a key in API keys. byoa reads INSTABOX_API_KEY. The free plan has 1 sandbox in all, also when it is stopped, so it is enough for 1 user's kept sandbox or 1 job (limits). - Sprites (Fly.io): sign up, then make a Sprites token of your organization (how). byoa reads SPRITES_TOKEN. A new account gets $1 of credit with no card; the Free plan gives $5 of usage a month and has 3 Sprites (pricing). - With the variable set, e2b(), daytona(), instabox() and sprites() read the key themselves. head: Make one agents object
text: Make one agents object in your backend: once for each process, or once in each Convex action. - app: lower-case letters, digits and -, at most 24. It names the app's sandboxes and login volumes. - sandbox: the sandbox provider. To change the provider, change this one line. - store: your own database, through a store adapter. For Postgres, run POSTGRES_SCHEMA once. - encryptionKey: 32 random bytes as base64. Keep it the same between restarts, and keep it secret. - proxyUrl: a public HTTPS URL. The sandbox must reach it. In development, use a tunnel such as cloudflared tunnel --url http://localhost:3000. The default E2B template is named byoa, and a new E2B account does not have it. Build it one time with buildE2BTemplate(), or pass e2b({ template: 'base' }). See Sandbox providers.

head: Serve two routes
text: byoa's handlers are fetch handlers (Request → Response). On Node, wrap your app's handler with toNodeListener from @madeyexz/byoa/node. - The proxy checks the job token itself. Do not put your app's session check in front of it: the harness in the sandbox has no app session. - Every other route reads the user from your app's own session. The userId you give byoa is your app's stable user id. Never take it from a header or a body that the browser controls.

head: Sign the user in to their plan
text: The sign-in runs the unmodified CLI in a sandbox. The user signs in on the lab's own page. byoa gives your app only that page's URL and, for Codex and Grok Build, a code. See AI login for each step. The sign-in's sandbox lives only while your sign-in UI checks in: each finishLogin call keeps it for 2 more minutes. For Claude Code, call finishLogin(userId, 'claude') with no code about every 30 seconds while the user is on Anthropic's page. A user with an OpenCode Go plan (beta) gives a key instead: agents.connectKey(userId, 'opencode-go', key). See AI login.

head: Connect an MCP tool, one time
text: Every later job of this user can have this server. Your app's own data needs no MCP server: give its tools to createAgents as functions. See MCP tools and the proxy.

head: Run a job
text: run does not throw when a job fails. It gives error events, then always one end event. See Running agents for the events, what the agent may do, and jobs at the same time.

text: skills/byoa is a skill in the Agent Skills format. It teaches a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Amp and others) to add byoa to an app: the install, createAgents with a store and a sandbox adapter, the sign-in, the MCP connections and their routes, agents.run and its events, and the lab rules. head: Sandbox lifecycle
text: This page shows every sandbox byoa creates, from creation to removal, with the default storedLogin(). A sandbox has the user's login files only while a sign-in, a job or a sign-out runs. When your backend dies during a job, a watcher in the sandbox removes them. byoa creates four kinds of sandbox: - a sign-in sandbox for each sign-in, which byoa never keeps. It ends at cancelLogin, or 2 minutes after your app's last finishLogin check-in, 15 minutes at most (AI login shows its steps); - a job sandbox: by default one kept sandbox for each user, harness and sandboxKey (a conversation is a key of its own), paused between jobs; or, with sandboxPer: 'job', a new one for each job; - a sign-out sandbox, for 5 minutes, where the CLI signs out (AI login); - a models sandbox for each agents.listModels call, where the CLI lists the models of the user's plan. byoa destroys it after the list, 10 minutes at most.

head: What carries over between jobs
text: "Resume" can mean two things. byoa does both: - Resume the sandbox. byoa starts the user's paused sandbox again for the next job. The files outside ~/work and the installed harness are still there. This happens in every kept sandbox. - Resume the conversation. Only for a job that names a conversation. The harness continues its own session, so the agent knows the earlier messages and what it did. Each CLI does this its own way: Claude Code --session-id, then --resume; Codex's app server keeps the thread, then resumes it (thread/resume); Grok Build's agent mode names a session, then resumes it (session/resume). While a job runs, it also takes more messages (job.send, see Running agents). text: close() never runs. byoa still loses little, and no login stays in the sandbox: Diagram: A job whose backend dies, with the default storedLogin 1. The job runs. About every 60 s, byoa saves what the CLI changed in its login (a checkpoint), with compare-and-set. The loan record ailoginloan/<user>/<h>/<sandbox> names the stored version this sandbox has. head: Removal
text: - agents.signOut(user, h) deletes the user's kept sandboxes for that harness, then signs out (AI login). - agents.deleteSandbox(user, { harness?, sandboxKey? }) on its own destroys each matching kept sandbox. A job in it ends. The login, the MCP grants and the conversations' stored transcripts stay. - agents.deleteConversation(user, conversation?) deletes a conversation (or all of the user's): its stored session and transcript, and its kept sandbox. Call it when the user deletes a chat, and with no id when you delete the user. When you delete a user, call agents.deleteSandbox(userId); when you delete a project that had a key, agents.deleteSandbox(userId, { sandboxKey: projectId }). - Nothing else removes a paused kept sandbox.

head: MCP tools and the proxy
text: The user connects each MCP tool one time, and every agent run that your app gives it has it. The real tokens stay in your database. The agent in the sandbox gets only a job token for your proxy.

head: Connect a server, one time for each user
text: - name: lower-case letters, digits and -, at most 32. A job asks for servers by this name. - The URL must be https:// (or http:// on localhost). With bearer, byoa checks the token with one MCP initialize, and throws if the server refuses it. - byoa uses Client ID Metadata Documents when the server supports them (serve agents.clientMetadata() at oauth.clientMetadataUrl), and Dynamic Client Registration only when it does not. - The server's sign-in page sends the browser to your oauth.redirectUrl route, which calls agents.finishMcp({ state, code, error }). It finds the user from the stored state, so that route needs no session. A sign-in that does not finish in 15 minutes runs out; call connectMcp again. - byoa refreshes each grant itself, with one refresh owner: your backend. Two jobs that need a refresh at the same time cause one refresh request: the refresh holds a lease in the store, and renews it while the authorization server answers. byoa asks the user to connect again only when the authorization server refuses the refresh token (a 4xx answer); a 5xx, a 429 or no answer fails that request only. Do not refresh or read the tokens in your app's code.

head: The proxy and job tokens
text: Serve agents.proxy at proxyUrl and at every path below it (<proxyUrl>/<name>). It is a fetch handler. For each job, byoa writes an MCP config in the sandbox that points to the proxy, with a job token for that one job and one user. - The proxy checks the job token, adds the user's real token, and sends the request on to the MCP server. - It refuses a job token after the job ends, and for a server that the job did not get. - Do not put your app's session check in front of it. Each of its answers has the header x-byoa-proxy: 1. - No real MCP token is in the sandbox's environment, files or processes at any time. A test checks this after each job with a real MCP call (V5). The same proxy is also the relay of a job on the user's OpenCode Go key (beta), at <proxyUrl>/_plan/opencode-go/…: it checks the job token, adds the user's key, and sends only the model requests on to OpenCode. So do not filter the paths below proxyUrl. See AI login. A job gets only the servers that your app names in its mcp. A server in mcp that the user has not connected gives an error event with code mcp, and the job runs without it.

head: When the proxy is down
text: Before the harness starts, byoa checks from the job's sandbox that each MCP server of the job answers through agents.proxy. When the sandbox cannot reach the proxy (a wrong proxyUrl, a tunnel that ended, a firewall), the job does not start: run gives an error event with code mcp and ends with ok: false, and session throws ProxyError. A server that does not answer gives an error event with code mcp, and the job runs. Without this check, a harness that cannot reach a server leaves its tools out and still ends well.

head: Your app's own tools
text: Give your app's own tools to createAgents as functions (tools): MCP server name → tool name → { description, input, run }. input is the JSON Schema of the arguments. A job gets them by the server's name in mcp, as it gets a connected server. The harness calls them through agents.proxy, which checks the job token and calls run(args, { user, job }) in your backend, for the user of that job. So you write no MCP server, keep no token for it, and connect nothing for each user. What run returns goes to the agent (a string as it is, other values as JSON); when it throws, the agent gets the message as a failed call. byoa does not check the arguments against input: check them in run.

head: Move a grant into byoa
text: To move an MCP grant that the user already made elsewhere into byoa, call agents.importMcp(userId, { name, url, oauth }) with the MCP SDK's state (client, tokens, at). Delete the old copy, so that the grant keeps one refresh owner.

head: Call a service's other API with the user's grant
text: Some MCP servers have an API next to the MCP endpoint that is not MCP, such as an export. Your backend calls it with the user's grant through agents.fetchWithGrant(userId, 'tasks', 'https://mcp.example.com/export'): byoa adds the current token, refreshed by the one refresh owner, and gives you the response. By default, it sends the token only to the origin of that grant's MCP server. It does not follow redirects, and never gives you the token. When the service's API is on another origin than its MCP server, name that origin in your own configuration, for the MCP server's origin. Only grants of that MCP server can go there, and only to that exact origin: The MCP server, the sandbox and the user cannot add an origin. Each one is an exact origin: https, no path, no wildcard.

head: Security
text: This page is SECURITY.md of the repository. byoa handles your users' AI logins and their MCP tokens. A bug in byoa can give an attacker access to a user's Notion, Gmail or AI plan. Please tell us about each security problem that you find.

head: Report a problem
text: - Do not open a public issue, pull request or discussion. - Use GitHub's private report: go to the Security tab of this repository and click Report a vulnerability. - Tell us what the problem is, how to make it occur, and what an attacker can get. - Do not put a real user's tokens or data in the report. Use test accounts. We will reply within 7 days. We will tell you when we fix the problem, and we will give you credit if you want it.

head: Supported versions
text: We fix security problems in the latest release on npm (@madeyexz/byoa).

head: Where secrets are kept
text: This is how byoa must keep each secret (see SPEC.md). If byoa does not do this, it is a security problem. Secret Where it is Where it must never be --------- The user's Claude or ChatGPT login By default in the app's own database, encrypted with a key that the app gives (R1.4), or as an option in a volume of that one user (R1.5); in a sandbox only while a sign-in, a job or a sign-out runs In a sandbox between jobs, in another app, or with us MCP grants (access and refresh tokens) In the app's own database, encrypted with a key that the app gives (R2.4) In the sandbox (R3.3), in logs, or with us Job token In the sandbox's mcp.json, for one job and one user (R3.1) Valid after the job ends (R3.4) A conversation's transcript (the harness's own session files) In the conversation's kept sandbox, and a copy in the app's own database, encrypted with a key that the app gives (R5.9) In the store without encryption, or in another user's sandbox The real MCP token goes only from the app's backend to the MCP server, through the proxy (R3.2). byoa is not a hosted service, so we never get your users' tokens.

head: What we count as a security problem
text: For example: - A real MCP token is in the sandbox's environment, files or processes (V5). - The proxy accepts a job token after its job ends (V6), or for a different user. - byoa keeps a copy of a user's AI login in a sandbox between jobs, stores it without encryption, or one app can use another app's login. - Two refreshes at the same time revoke a grant, or byoa sends a refresh request from a place other than the app's backend (R2.3). - byoa stores a grant or a conversation's transcript without encryption, or writes a token to a log. - byoa runs a claude or codex binary that is not the published one (V11).

head: What is not ours
text: Report these to their owners: - Bugs in a sandbox provider (E2B, Daytona, Instabox, Sprites), in Claude Code or Codex, or in an MCP server. - Bugs in an app that uses byoa, for example a leaked encryption key or a database that is open to the internet. The app must keep its encryption key secret and keep the proxy in its own backend.

head: AI login
text: A user's AI login stays encrypted in your app's database, and is in a sandbox only while a sign-in, a job or a sign-out runs. This page shows how byoa signs a user in to Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build, keeps the CLI's own login files, and uses them for each job. An OpenCode Go plan (beta) has no sign-in: the user gives a key, which never goes into the sandbox (below). The login tokens are in They are never in ------ the sign-in sandbox, until byoa destroys it what byoa returns to your app your app's database, encrypted the job's environment variables a job's sandbox, only while the job runs a kept sandbox between jobs the state, lease, line and loan entries in the store This is for the default login, storedLogin(). With cliLogin, the tokens stay in the user's volume instead of the database. byoa never uses the tokens itself and never calls the labs' token endpoints. The unmodified CLI is the only client that sends them to the lab.

head: Where the login stays between jobs
text: In your app's database (the default, storedLogin()) In a volume of the user (cliLogin) --------- How it gets there byoa reads the CLI's files from the sign-in sandbox and encrypts them together with AES-256-GCM, with your encryptionKey or the key you give storedLogin. The entry's name is part of the encryption, so the entry cannot be moved to another user. The sign-in sandbox mounts the user's volume at ~/.claude or ~/.codex, and the CLI writes its files there. Where it is one entry for each user and harness, ailogin/<user>/<harness>, as v1.<iv>.<ciphertext>. It is the only copy between jobs. the volume byoa-<app>-<harness>-<first 24 hex of sha256(user)>, with the files as the CLI wrote them In a job byoa copies the files in and takes them out again (below). Every job sandbox of that user and harness mounts the same volume. byoa never reads or copies the files. The store keeps only the state. Providers all providers with volumes: E2B (when volumes are on for your team) and Daytona, not Instabox or Sprites To keep the logins in a table of their own, with a key of their own, so that you can give them their own access rules and backups, see Stores and Convex. To use the volume, pass login: cliLogin (from @madeyexz/byoa). The labs' published terms limit where these tokens may be stored. Each app checks them: see Lab rules.

head: Sign-out
text: agents.signOut(user, harness) deletes the user's kept sandboxes for this harness, signs out with the CLI so that the lab can revoke the login, and deletes the login. Diagram: Sign-out, with the default storedLogin 1. Destroy the user's kept sandboxes for this harness. signOut(user, h) calls deleteSandbox(user, { harness: h }). A job in one of them ends. Login files: no login files. 2. Question: Is a login stored? ailogin/<user>/<h>. If yes: go on to step 3. - If no: Skip the CLI sign-out. Then go on to step 5. 3. Sign out with the CLI in a new sandbox. Takes the login lease alone, writes the files in, and runs claude auth logout, codex logout or grok logout, so that the lab can revoke the login. If this fails, byoa goes on. Time limit: 5 min; not kept; waits in line for the lease. Login files: login files in. 4. Destroy it, give the lease back. Login files: no login files. 5. Delete the stored login. The state is 'signed-out'. This is the end. ailogin/<user>/<h> is deleted. With cliLogin, sign-out also destroys an unfinished sign-in sandbox, signs out in a sandbox that mounts the user's volume, and deletes the volume.

head: Give your agent tools
text: The agent in each job is the user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build. You decide what it can do in that job: which tools it can call, what it knows, and what it may do in its sandbox. This page shows each way, and which one to choose. The agent needs Give it Where it runs Who connects it ------------ your app's own data and actions (to-dos, mail, documents) your app's tools, as functions in createAgents({ tools }) in your backend nobody: the job token says which user a service where the user has an account (Notion, Gmail) the user's MCP server, with connectMcp once at the service the user, one time to know how to do a task, or your app's rules skills and AGENTS.md, in setup files in the sandbox nobody skills and MCP servers as one package a plugin (Agent Plugins 1.0), in plugins files, and the user's servers the user, for each server a shell, files, packages and the network the sandbox itself, with access: 'full' in the sandbox nobody Name the tools of each job in its mcp. A job gets only the servers that you name, and none by default.

head: Which one to choose
text: Diagram: Which way gives the agent an ability 1. Question: Is it your app's own data or action? If no: go on to step 2. - If yes: Your app's own tools. This is the end. tools: { todos: { add_todo: { description, input, run } } }, and mcp: ['todos'] in the job. 2. Question: Does the user have an account at a service with an MCP server? If no: go on to step 3. - If yes: The user's MCP server. This is the end. connectMcp(user, url, { name }) once, and mcp: ['notion'] in each job. 3. Question: Is it knowledge, a how-to or a rule, not an action? If no: go on to step 4. - If yes: A skill or AGENTS.md. This is the end. setup: { agentsMd, skills }. The harness reads them from the job folder. 4. Question: Does it need a shell, files, packages or the open network? If no: go on to step 5. - If yes: The sandbox, with access: 'full'. This is the end. The default. The agent installs and runs what it needs in its own sandbox. 5. Write it as one of your app's tools. This is the end. An API that your backend can call becomes a function in tools. The agent then calls it through the proxy, and your backend keeps every key. Keep secrets out of the sandbox. A key that a tool needs stays in your backend, in the tool's run or in the user's grant. Never put a token in setup, the task, the environment or a file: the agent can read everything in its sandbox.

head: Your app's own tools
text: Give your app's tools to createAgents as functions: MCP server name → tool name → { description, input, run }. A job gets a group by its name in mcp, as it gets a connected server. You write no MCP server, keep no token for it, and connect nothing for each user. Diagram: A call to one of your app's tools 1. The agent calls todos.add_todo. The harness sends an MCP tools/call to <proxyUrl>/todos, with the job token. 2. Question: Is the job token good, and did the job get todos? If yes: go on to step 3. - If no: Refuse the call. This is the end. The job ended, or its mcp did not name todos. 3. run(args, { user, job }) in your backend. user is the job's user, from the token. Never take the user from the arguments. 4. Question: Did run throw? If no: go on to step 5. - If yes: The agent gets a failed call. This is the end. With the error's message. The agent can try again or tell the user. 5. The agent gets the result. This is the end. A string as it is, and any other value as JSON. - input is the JSON Schema of the arguments, which the harness shows to the model. byoa does not check the arguments against it: check them in run. - Write a description that says when to use the tool. The model reads it to choose. - Names: a server is lower-case letters, digits and -, at most 32; a tool is letters, digits, _ and -, at most 64. - Give a job only the groups it needs. A to-do job gets todos, not your billing tools.

head: The user's MCP servers
text: The user connects a service one time, and each job that you give it can use it. The real token stays in your database, and the proxy adds it to each call. MCP tools and the proxy has the sign-in routes and the details. Diagram: A call to the user's MCP server 1. The agent calls notion.search. To <proxyUrl>/notion, with the job token. The sandbox has no Notion token. 2. Question: Is the job token good, and did the job get notion? If yes: go on to step 3. - If no: Refuse the call. This is the end. 3. Take the user's grant. From your database, decrypted in your backend. byoa refreshes it first when it is due, with one refresh owner. 4. Send the call on to Notion's MCP server. This is the end. With the real token. The answer goes back to the agent; the token does not. A server in mcp that the user has not connected gives an error event with code mcp, and the job runs without it. Before the harness starts, byoa checks from the sandbox that each server answers through the proxy (When the proxy is down).

head: Skills and AGENTS.md
text: A skill teaches the agent how to do one kind of task, in the Agent Skills format: a folder with a SKILL.md and any files it needs. AGENTS.md has the rules for every task of the job, such as your app's voice or what the agent must not do. byoa writes them into a new job folder, where each harness reads them:

head: Plugins
text: A plugin in the Agent Plugins 1.0 format is a folder with plugin.json, skills/<name>/ and mcp.json. Read it with readPlugin(readPluginDir(dir)) (readPluginDir from @madeyexz/byoa/node), and give it to a job in plugins: - The job gets the plugin's skills, and each of its MCP servers through the user's grant of the same name. So the user connects each server with connectMcp under that name; byoa never gives the plugin's URL to the harness, only the proxy's. - Only Streamable HTTP servers load. A stdio server would run inside the sandbox with no proxy, so byoa skips it and lists it in plugin.skipped.

head: What the agent can do in its sandbox
text: With access: 'full' (the default), the agent has every tool of its harness, with no approval: a shell, file changes and the network. So it can install a package, run a script, clone a repository or call a public API, in a sandbox that is the job's alone. - Files stay in a kept sandbox. With the default sandboxPer: 'user', files that the agent writes outside ~/work are there in the user's next job. The job folder ~/work is new each time. With sandboxPer: 'job', nothing stays. See Sandbox lifecycle. - Results come back as events. The agent's answer is the end event's result, and its tool calls are tool_call and tool_result events. To get a file out, give the agent a tool that saves it, such as save_report in your tools, or open the job with agents.session and read the file yourself with s.sandbox.run. - Limit it with access: 'read-only' when the agent needs only its MCP tools, such as in a mail client. It can then call the job's MCP tools and read files, but not change a file or reach the network by itself. See Running agents.

head: Running agents
text: Your app runs a job with agents.run. byoa takes the user's sandbox, loads the user's setup, runs the user's own harness on the user's own plan, and streams its events. To continue a chat, give its jobs one conversation id. For a program of your own around the harness, use agents.session; for a harness outside byoa's sandboxes, agents.jobToken.

head: Run a job and stream its events
text: - The events are the same for every harness. The schema is in the API reference. - run does not throw when a job fails. It gives error events (code: signed-out, expired, no-plan, usage-limit, rate-limited, harness, sandbox, mcp or conversation), and always ends with one end event (ok, result, usage, and in a conversation session). On signed-out or expired, show the sign-in again (for plan: 'opencode-go', ask for a new key). On no-plan, tell the user that the key's workspace has no OpenCode Go plan. On usage-limit and rate-limited, see When the plan is used up. - byoa writes skills where each harness reads them (.claude/skills/, .agents/skills/), AGENTS.md (and CLAUDE.md for Claude Code) from one source, and the MCP config in each harness's own format. plugins adds the skills and MCP servers of an Agent Plugins package (readPlugin(readPluginDir(dir))). - byoa installs the pinned version of each harness in each sandbox, so a new pin reaches every user at their next job. - If the client goes away, stop the loop (or call return() on the generator). byoa still ends the job token, takes the login out, and pauses or destroys the sandbox.

head: When the plan is used up
text: Each plan has limits: Claude's and ChatGPT's 5-hour and weekly limits, Grok's plan limit, OpenCode Go's 5-hour, weekly and monthly limits. When the user's plan is used up, the job ends with an error of code usage-limit. Its resetsAt (ms since 1970) is when the plan resets, when the tool says: Claude Code and Codex say it, and for OpenCode Go byoa asks OpenCode's usage meter; Grok Build does not say it. message is the tool's own words. byoa keeps the used-up plan in the store, for that user and harness (with plan: 'opencode-go', for that user and plan, with both harnesses), until resetsAt, or for 15 minutes when the tool did not say. Until then, a job of that user and harness ends at once with the same error, and starts no sandbox. To check before a job, with no sandbox: A new sign-in (finishLogin that says signed-in), a new key (connectKey), signOut, and a job that works end it. One user's plan is one user's: an app that runs every visitor on one user's login (such as byoa's own help agent) gets one check for all of them. rate-limited is a refusal for now: too many requests, or the lab is overloaded. byoa keeps nothing; try again in a moment. A login that the lab refuses is expired, as before. byoa reads each CLI's own code first, and its words only when the code is missing: Claude Code's API error and its rate_limit_event, Codex's codexErrorInfo and its rate limits, Grok Build's error_kind. These checks use output in the shape that each pinned binary writes; no check has run

head: What the agent may do
text: By default (access: 'full'), the agent has every tool of its harness, with no approval: a shell, file changes and the network. This is for a sandbox that is the job's alone. An app whose agent must only use its MCP tools, such as a to-do list or a mail client, gives the job access: 'read-only': The agent can then call the job's MCP tools and read files, so the harness can still read its skills and AGENTS.md. It cannot change a file or reach the network by itself. byoa only sets each CLI's own options: Codex runs in its own sandbox with a read-only permission profile, which also denies its commands Codex's home folder (CODEX_HOME), where its login is, Claude Code gets only its tools that read, and Grok Build gets rules that deny its shell, file changes and web fetch (and its web search finds nothing); each tool a CLI refuses is a permission event or an error for the model. Apart from Codex's home folder, read-only does not hide files: the agent can read each file that its user can read, also Claude Code's and Grok Build's login files. Use it always with localSandbox() on a user's own computer, where the sandbox isolates nothing.

head: Sandbox modes
text: Where a job runs Jobs of one user and harness at the same time --------- sandboxPer: 'user' (the default) the user's one kept sandbox for that harness, paused between jobs one; the others wait in line, in the order they came a sandboxKey for each job one kept sandbox for each key, such as a project or a conversation, each with its own lease one for each key a conversation for each job one kept sandbox for each conversation, whose ~/work stays one for each conversation sandboxPer: 'job' a new sandbox, destroyed after the job all of them A job waits in line with no time limit. To make it fail after a time, set createAgents({ waitMs }), for example on a short-lived backend such as a Convex action. Sandbox lifecycle shows each step of each mode, and what each provider does.

head: Conversations
text: A job with a conversation id continues the harness's own session of the earlier jobs with that id, so the agent knows what the user said and what it did. Use your chat thread's id: - The first job's start event has resumed: false, the next ones resumed: true. The end event has session, the harness's own session id. - The conversation has its own kept sandbox (its id is the sandboxKey; give no other one), so its jobs run one at a time, and its ~/work stays from job to job: the agent finds the files it wrote. byoa replaces only its own files there. - byoa keeps a copy of the transcript, encrypted in your store, so the conversation goes on when the provider loses the sandbox. A transcript longer than createAgents({ transcriptBytes }) (default 700 000 bytes) is not kept; then a lost sandbox loses the conversation, and the next job gives an error with code conversation and starts again. - agents.deleteConversation(userId, chatId) deletes it, with its sandbox. Sandbox lifecycle has what carries over between jobs. - The harness must be the same for each job of a conversation: each harness has its own sessions.

head: More messages while a job runs (steering)
text: run returns a Job. job.send(message) gives the running agent one more message, with each harness: Codex and Grok Build take a message that comes during a turn into that turn: the agent reads it at its next step, and answers both in the same turn. Claude Code takes it when the turn ends, as the next turn. A message that comes after a turn ended starts the next turn. byoa uses only each CLI's own protocol, through a small driver script in the sandbox: Claude Code's stream-json input, Codex's app server (turn/steer) and Grok Build's Agent Client Protocol (x.ai/interject). Once the job ended, send returns false: send the message as the next job of the conversation.

head: Jobs at the same time
text: Your app chooses how one user's agents run. It can mix the three ways: - A queue. onWait gets { for, ahead } each time the number of jobs ahead changes. for is 'sandbox' while the job waits for its sandbox, and 'login' while it waits for the AI login. - Several messages. byoa gives the agent all of them in one task, with a line that tells it to read them all first and then decide the order. It is one job, in one sandbox. - Several sandboxes. Jobs of one user in different sandboxes run at the same time with one sign-in, for every harness. They share the login while it is not due for a refresh. One risk stays, and storedLogin({ parallel: false }) turns sharing off: see AI login.

head: Models and effort
text: run(userId, { harness, task, model, effort }) runs the harness with that model and effort, with each CLI's own flags: Claude Code's --model (an alias such as opus, or a full name) and --effort (low to max), Codex's -m and model_reasoning_effort, Grok Build's -m and --reasoning-effort. Without them, a job gets the harness's default from createAgents({ models }), else the CLI's own. agents.listModels(userId, harness) lists the models that the user's plan can use, as the CLI lists them with the user's login: [{ id, name, description, isDefault, efforts, resolved? }]. id is what model takes, and efforts what effort takes; resolved (Claude Code) is the full name of an alias. Each call starts a sandbox, so keep the list for a while. It throws LoginError when the harness is not signed in. With session, s.args has the flags for the job's model and effort, for your own command line. A job on the user's OpenCode Go key (beta) passes plan: 'opencode-go' and a Go model; listModels(userId, 'opencode-go') lists them with no sandbox. See AI login.

head: A program of your own around the harness
text: An app that runs its own program around the unmodified harness (for example its own server, which starts claude, codex or grok itself) opens the job with agents.session instead. It gets the same sandbox, login, pinned harness and job token, and runs its own command: session throws LoginError when the harness is not signed in, and ProxyError when the sandbox cannot reach the proxy.

head: A harness outside byoa's sandboxes
text: A program outside byoa's sandboxes, such as a harness on the user's own computer, gets a job token with no sandbox: const t = await agents.jobToken(userId, { mcp: ['notion'] }) gives t.token and t.mcp (the proxy URLs), with the same rules as a job's token, until t.close(). Send t.token as Authorization: Bearer to each t.mcp[].url.

head: E2B
text: Use e2b({ apiKey?, template?, timeoutMs? }). It needs the e2b package. - The default template is named byoa, and a new E2B account does not have it: the first job then fails with 404: template 'byoa' not found. Build it one time for each pin change with buildE2BTemplate(), or pass e2b({ template: 'base' }). Any template with Node 20 or later works: byoa then installs the pinned harness in each new sandbox (about 10 seconds). - pause ends the sandbox's processes, then takes a full snapshot, with the memory: the next job's resume takes about 0.3 seconds, and node and the harness start warm. When E2B refuses it, because it still saves the sandbox's previous snapshot, byoa takes a snapshot of the files only; the next resume then boots the sandbox again and reads its disk cold, which can add 10 to 20 seconds. E2B keeps a paused sandbox with no time limit, and charges no compute for it. - A kept sandbox that times out (a crash, a lost network) is paused, not killed. When byoa resumes a sandbox that paused itself, it ends any old process first.

head: Daytona
text: Use daytona({ apiKey?, client?, snapshot?, volume?, timeoutMs? }). It needs @daytona/sdk. - pause stops the sandbox, and resume starts it, also from archived (more slowly). A kept sandbox is not ephemeral and has no time to live; Daytona archives it after 7 days stopped. A sandbox for one job is ephemeral: Daytona deletes it when it stops, and at the latest after its time. - Daytona allows 100 volumes for each organization, so with cliLogin the adapter keeps every user's AI login in its own subpath of one shared volume (byoa by default). A sandbox mounts only that user's subpath. - On Daytona Tier 1 and Tier 2, a sandbox can reach only allowed domains, so serve agents.proxy on one of them (for example .convex.site), or use Tier 3 or higher. .workers.dev is on Daytona's list but does not work: a Worker's address has two labels below it (<worker>.<account>.workers.dev), and Daytona does not resolve those.

head: Instabox
text: Use instabox({ apiKey?, apiUrl?, template?, snapshot?, timeoutMs? }). It calls Instabox's HTTP API itself, so it needs no package. - Each sandbox starts from the agent-browser template (Node 22, user user, home /data/home), or from a snapshot that you name (snapshot). - byoa stops the user's sandbox after each job (not Instabox's pause), so the next job starts it again with its files and no process of the last one. A sandbox that paused itself (idle for 30 minutes, or at the plan's longest run) is booted again. A sandbox for one job is deleted after it, and at the latest at its timeoutMs. - byoa gives a sandbox none of your account's Vault items or org Secrets, and leaves its commands out of Instabox's command history, which would otherwise keep their output (and so the AI login that byoa reads back). - Instabox has no volumes, so cliLogin does not work there; the default stored login does. Instabox sandboxes reach every public domain, so a tunnel works for proxyUrl. - On the free plan, a workspace has one sandbox in all, also when it is stopped (so one user with one kept sandbox, or one job), and three starts a minute (byoa waits when Instabox answers 429). A run starts with 2 hours before Instabox pauses the sandbox, and grows to 8 hours at most while the sandbox is in use (limits).

head: Sprites
text: Use sprites({ token?, apiUrl?, init?, timeoutMs? }). A Sprite is a Linux VM of Fly.io with a disk that stays. The adapter calls the Sprites API itself, so it needs no package. Make a Sprites token of your Fly.io organization (how), and set it as SPRITES_TOKEN. - Each Sprite has Ubuntu, Node, git and the labs' CLIs; user sprite, home /home/sprite. byoa still installs its pinned harness (about 5 seconds). Sprites has no templates: to add what your jobs need, such as a clone of a repository, pass a shell command as init, which runs once in each new Sprite, with the network and sudo. - A Sprite sleeps by itself about 30 seconds after nothing runs in it, also when a process of byoa still has work, such as the watcher that takes the AI login out (R1.4). So the adapter holds each Sprite awake until its time, with the Tasks API in the Sprite: a sandbox's timeoutMs, setTimeout and keepAlive work as on E2B. At its time, a kept Sprite sleeps with its files; one that is not kept stops its processes and deletes its home folder, and the next create deletes it at Sprites. - pause ends the job's processes and lets the Sprite sleep, so the next job wakes it in about a second, with its files. When byoa resumes a Sprite whose time ran out (your backend died during a job), it ends any old process first. - A Sprite's user has some Linux capabilities, such as CAP_SYS_ADMIN. byoa runs each command with none, so the agent has no more power than an ordinary user, and Codex's own sandbox, which access

head: The local sandbox
text: localSandbox({ root?, volumes?, env? }) is folders on this computer. It isolates nothing: use it only for development and tests, and with access: 'read-only' for a harness on a user's own computer. On macOS, the Codex sign-in works in it; the Claude Code sign-in needs Linux.

head: Write an adapter
text: An adapter implements one interface (src/sandbox/types.ts): create (with volumes), resume, run a command, write a file, pause, destroy, delete a volume, and optionally read a file, set a running sandbox's time again (Sandbox.setTimeout), capabilities, and keepAlive (a new end time for a sandbox that is not kept: byoa uses it to end a sign-in 2 minutes after the app's last check-in). - keep: true is a sandbox that byoa keeps for the user. When it times out, the provider must pause it instead of deleting it, and no process of that job may run when it resumes. - A provider with no volumes refuses create with volumes, and says capabilities: { volumes: false }. - run resolves for a non-zero exit code, and with exit code 137 for a command that runs out of its timeoutMs; it does not throw. - Sandbox.readFile(path) (optional) reads a file through the provider's file API, or gives null. byoa reads the login files and a conversation's transcript with it; without it, byoa reads them as base64 on a command's output, which a provider may keep in its command history. - Sandbox.setTimeout(ms) (optional) sets the provider's time of a running sandbox again, ms from now, as timeoutMs at create: then a kept sandbox pauses, and another one ends. byoa calls it when a job has the user's AI login, so the time the job waited in line for the login does not count. - test/helpers/conformance.ts in byoa's repository checks what byoa needs of an adapter: run it on yours, as test/fake.test.ts does for the

head: Stores and Convex
text: byoa keeps its state in your own database, through a store adapter: MCP grants, AI logins (by default), login states, sandbox slots and leases, and conversations (the harness's session id and a copy of its transcript). Grants, AI logins and conversations are encrypted with your encryptionKey.

head: The store adapter
text: A store is four methods. byoa ships one for Postgres, one for Convex and one in memory for tests. For another database, write your own. The version must change on every write, and a key that is deleted and written again must never get an earlier version back. Each call must take effect at one instant, and get must answer the latest write: do not send it to a read replica or a cache, or a job that came later can take a sandbox or a login first, and an index can lose an entry. Do not send a write again after an error (a retry wrapper): the first one may have written. The one refresh owner of each grant, the login lease and the sandbox slots depend on cas. The to-do example's sqliteStore in examples/todo/todos.ts is one in 19 lines.

head: The keys byoa writes
text: Every key is in one file, src/keys.ts. The values marked sealed are encrypted with your encryptionKey, with the key as associated data; the others hold no secret. <user> and the sandbox key are URL-encoded. Key What it holds ------ grant/<user>/<name> sealed: one MCP grant grants/<user> the names and URLs of the user's grants lease/<user>/<name> the lease of the one refresh of a grant mcpflow/<state> sealed: an MCP sign-in that has not come back yet job/<hash>, jobid/<job> a job token, by its hash, and its hash by the job id login/<user>/<h>, loginjob/<user>/<h> the state of a lab login; a sign-in that runs now ailogin/<user>/<h> sealed: the CLI's own login files ailoginlease/…, ailoginline/…, ailoginloan/… who holds the login, the jobs that wait for it, and the sandboxes that have a copy aikey/<user>/<plan>, aikeystate/<user>/<plan> sealed: a plan's key; its state usersandbox/<user>/<provider>/<h>/<key> (and …/line) a kept sandbox: its id and the lease of its job; the jobs that wait for it usersandboxes/<user>/<provider> the user's kept sandboxes conversation/<user>/<h>/<id> sealed: a conversation's session id and its transcript (at most transcriptBytes) conversations/<user> the user's conversations A conversation's transcript can be large: with the default transcriptBytes (700 000) one entry stays below a Convex document's 1 MiB. Postgres has no such limit.

head: Convex
text: In a Convex app, byoa's state is one table and four internal functions in your deployment (@madeyexz/byoa/store/convex). Call byoa from actions and HTTP actions, which can make network calls; serve agents.proxy from an HTTP action. A Convex action has a time limit, and a job waits in line with no limit by default, so set waitMs shorter than the action's limit. On Daytona Tier 1 and 2, .convex.site is an allowed domain for the proxy.

head: A table of its own for the AI logins
text: To keep the logins in a table of their own, with a key of their own, so that you can give them their own access rules and backups: To keep each login in a volume of that user and app instead, behind the sandbox adapter, pass login: cliLogin (from @madeyexz/byoa). Your database then never holds the login. This needs a provider with volumes; see AI login.

head: Test your app without a plan or a sandbox
text: Use harness: 'fake', localSandbox() from @madeyexz/byoa/sandbox/local and memoryStore() from @madeyexz/byoa. The fake harness runs no model and needs no login. It reads the same MCP config Claude Code would, and calls MCP tools through the real proxy: each task line call <server>.<tool> <json> is one call. So a test proves your app's routes, grants and proxy end to end. - The fake harness shows the task's first line as one text event and skips the other lines. The last call's output is the end event's result. - In a conversation, the fake harness keeps each task in a session file and says how many earlier messages it remembers (fake harness remembers 1 earlier messages: <first line>), so you test your app's conversations with no model. - With the local sandbox, proxyUrl can be http://127.0.0.1:<port>/byoa/mcp. - Copy examples/todo/todo.test.ts. Do not offer fake to end users in production.

head: Supported AI subscriptions
text: Your users bring an AI subscription that they already pay for. byoa runs it in the lab's own, unmodified CLI: Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build. Subscription Plans that work Can the user's account get banned? --------- Claude, in Claude Code Pro, Max, Ultra, Team and Enterprise. Not Free. It can. Anthropic's terms forbid apps to store Claude logins, and Anthropic may act without notice. ChatGPT, in Codex Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu. Not Free or Go. It can. OpenAI's terms want the login kept where the user controls it, and paid or hosted apps must apply to be partners. Grok, in Grok Build SuperGrok and X Premium+ Unclear. xAI's terms forbid sharing an account and "unauthorized automated" access, and say nothing about apps that run Grok Build for their users. OpenCode Go (beta), in Claude Code or Codex Go, Go Plus and Go Teams It can. OpenCode's terms say "only for your own internal use". Why, and what to do before you launch: Can my user's AI account get banned? - Claude, ChatGPT and Grok: the user signs in on the lab's own page. See AI login. - OpenCode Go (beta): the user gives a key from OpenCode's Console, and the key never goes into the sandbox. No real Go key has run it yet. See AI login. - Prices and limits: the labs change them often, so read their own pages, linked in the table.

head: What every plan has in common
text: - The user's plan limits apply. A job uses the same allowance as the user's own chats and coding: the five-hour and weekly limits are shared. When the user is at a limit, the CLI refuses, and the job ends with an error event. - One plan for each harness. A user can sign in to each of them, and each job names its harness: harness: 'claude', 'codex' or 'grok'. A job on the user's OpenCode Go key also names plan: 'opencode-go'. - The login belongs to your app. A login that a user made in your app is only for your app. Another app on byoa needs its own sign-in. See Lab rules. - The labs' terms apply. The labs restrict where an app may store the login, and OpenAI asks paid or hosted apps to apply to be partners. Read the FAQ before you launch.

head: What byoa does not support
text: - API keys. byoa signs in only with a plan. The one key it takes is the user's OpenCode Go key, which is a plan's key. An app that wants to pay for the AI with its own API key does not need byoa for the login. - Other labs' plans, such as Gemini or Kimi memberships. byoa runs only Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build in version 1. Gemini or Antigravity may come later. OpenCode is also an agent itself (the opencode CLI), but byoa does not run it in version 1: an OpenCode Go plan runs in Claude Code or Codex. - Sharing one login between apps. The labs do not allow it, and byoa keeps each app's logins apart (app in createAgents).

head: Lab rules
text: byoa runs the labs' own CLIs on each user's own plan, so byoa and every app on it follow the labs' published rules. This page has the rules from SPEC.md, and what each app must do.

head: Rules we follow
text: - We run the real, unmodified claude, codex and grok binaries. We never pretend to be another client. A test checks the hash of the installed binaries against the published packages (V11). - The user signs in through Anthropic's, OpenAI's or xAI's own sign-in page. - One app's AI login is used only by that app. - For OpenCode Go (beta), byoa uses only the user's own key, with OpenCode's documented API and the harness's own user agent, never OpenCode's Console CLI sign-in. OpenCode's terms do not clearly allow an app to run it for its users, so each app asks OpenCode first. - The labs' terms restrict where an AI login may be stored. byoa keeps it in your database by default, so each app checks those terms and signs its own agreements with the labs.

head: What is byoa?
text: byoa, short for "bring your own agent", is the simplest way to let your users bring their own AI subscription to power the agents in your app. Each user signs in to their own AI plan one time: Claude (in Claude Code), ChatGPT (in Codex), Grok (in Grok Build) or OpenCode Go (beta). When your app has work for the AI, byoa runs that user's own Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build in a sandbox on your E2B, Daytona or Instabox account, with the user's tools, and streams the result back. The user's plan pays for the AI. Your app pays only for the sandbox. byoa is an open-source library (Apache 2.0), the npm package @madeyexz/byoa. It runs inside your app's own backend, on Node or Bun. It is not a hosted service. See Why and when you need byoa and Getting started.

head: Can my user's AI account get banned?
text: It can. byoa cannot promise that it will not, because the labs decide, and their terms allow parts of what byoa does but not all of it. byoa is built to stay inside the parts that the labs allow: - It runs the labs' own CLIs, unmodified. The agent is the real Claude Code, Codex or Grok Build, installed from the labs' own npm packages, and a test checks the binaries against those packages (V11). byoa never pretends to be another client, and never calls the labs' APIs with the user's tokens. - The user signs in on the lab's own page, with the CLI's own sign-in. byoa never sees a password. - Each user uses their own plan, for their own work, and one app's login is only for that app. Anthropic's Claude Code legal and compliance page allows "an end user signing in to the unmodified Claude Code binary with their own Claude subscription, including where a platform hosts Claude Code". But the same page also says: - developers "may not collect, store, or intermediate Claude.ai credentials or session tokens". byoa's default login stores the CLI's login files, encrypted, in your app's database (AI login). - "Advertised usage limits for Pro, Max, and Ultra plans assume ordinary, individual usage of Claude Code". An app that runs many jobs for one user can go beyond that. - Anthropic "reserves the right to take measures to enforce these restrictions and may do so without prior notice." OpenAI's Sign in with ChatGPT Terms say that stored tokens "must be local and under the user's control,

head: What happens when the user's plan runs out?
text: The job ends with an error of code usage-limit, and resetsAt when the tool says when the plan resets (Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode Go say it; Grok Build does not). byoa keeps this until the reset, or for 15 minutes when it does not know the time. Until then, a job of that user and harness ends at once and starts no sandbox, so a used-up plan does not cost you a sandbox for each try. agents.usageLimit(userId, harness) tells you before a job. A refusal for now, such as a lab that is overloaded, is rate-limited: try again in a moment. See When the plan is used up.

head: Can one user run many agents at the same time?
text: Yes, with one sign-in, for Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build. Give each agent its own sandbox: a sandboxKey for each, or sandboxPer: 'job'. The jobs then share the user's login while it is not due for a refresh. Jobs in one sandbox wait in line instead, and one job can also carry several messages to one agent. See Running agents. All these jobs use the same plan, so they reach the plan's limits sooner. One risk stays with a shared login: when the lab answers 401 to two sandboxes at the same time, both CLIs refresh, one refresh fails, and the user may have to sign in again. storedLogin({ parallel: false }) turns sharing off (AI login). Jobs on an OpenCode Go key have no such risk: a key does not rotate.

head: Does the agent remember earlier jobs?
text: Only in a conversation. A job with a conversation id continues the harness's own session of the earlier jobs with that id, in the conversation's own kept sandbox, and its job folder (~/work) stays. A job with no conversation starts a new session, and its job folder is new. byoa keeps a copy of each conversation's transcript, encrypted in your database, so the agent still remembers when the provider loses the sandbox. A running job of each harness also takes more messages (job.send): Codex and Grok Build into the turn that runs, Claude Code after it. See Running agents and what carries over between jobs.

head: Which model does a job use?
text: The model and effort that you give run, else the harness's default from createAgents({ models }), else the CLI's own default. agents.listModels(userId, harness) lists the models that the user's plan can use, and the efforts of each, as the CLI lists them with the user's login. Pick from that list, because each plan has its own models. A job on an OpenCode Go key (beta) needs a Go model: agents.listModels(userId, 'opencode-go') lists them from OpenCode's API, with no sandbox. See Running agents.

head: What does an AI job cost with byoa, and with an API key?
text: Your app passes its AI costs on to its users, in its price, so the question is what each user pays. With an API key, your app buys every token at API prices. With byoa, the user's own plan pays for the model, and your app passes on only the sandbox. For 100 small tasks a month, that takes each user's cost from $24.50 to $49 with a frontier model, or from $3 with a cheap open-weight model and a worse agent, down to $1.38 on E2B, and a frontier agent on the plan they already pay for.

text: Take a small task in an AI-native app, such as "add these three to-dos and sort them by date". The agent makes about 20 model calls. Each call sends the conversation so far, so the inputs add up to about 500,000 tokens, of which about 90% are cache hits. The agent writes about 10,000 tokens, with its reasoning. The job takes about 5 minutes of sandbox time, from start to close(). These are estimates. head: What the numbers leave out
text: - Plan fees at the provider. E2B's Pro plan is $150 a month, and Instabox's Pro plan is $20 a month with $20 of usage in it. Daytona has no plan fee, and Sprites' Free plan has none (it gives $5 of usage a month). Sprites bills the CPU and memory that a job uses, not what it could use, so a job that mostly waits for the model costs less than the table says. - A kept sandbox between jobs. A paused or stopped sandbox costs no compute. It can cost a little for its disk: Daytona bills disk past the first 5 GiB. - The sign-in sandbox, once for each user and harness, for a few minutes. - An agent with no sandbox. An agent that only calls your app's own API, with no shell and no files, can run as an agent loop of your own, such as on AWS Lambda, with no sandbox. Then an API key costs only the tokens. byoa needs a sandbox, because Claude Code, Codex and Grok Build need a shell. - The user's plan has limits. A user who runs many long tasks reaches the five-hour or weekly limit of their plan, and the jobs stop until it resets.

head: createAgents(options)
text: - oauth.redirectUrl: the app's route that calls finishMcp. - oauth.clientMetadataUrl: an HTTPS URL where the app serves agents.clientMetadata() (a Client ID Metadata Document). Without it, byoa uses only Dynamic Client Registration. - oauth.clientName: the name the MCP server shows on its consent page. Default: app. - sandboxPer: 'user' (the default): the first job of a user and harness creates the user's sandbox; byoa pauses it after each job (E2B pause, Daytona and Instabox stop, Sprites sleep) and resumes it for the next, with a new job folder. One job of a user and harness at a time; the others wait in line, in the order they came. A job's sandboxKey (in run and session) gives the user one kept sandbox, with its own lease, for each key. A sandbox the provider no longer has is replaced by a new one. 'job': a new sandbox for each job, destroyed after it. With the default storedLogin(), a user's jobs in different sandboxes run at the same time with one login, for every harness. - models: the model and effort a job of each harness gets when it names none. Default: the CLI's own. See listModels. - transcriptBytes: after each job of a conversation, byoa keeps a copy of the harness's session files (its transcript), encrypted in the store, when they are at most this large, so the conversation goes on when the provider loses its sandbox. Default 700 000 bytes, below a Convex document's 1 MiB. A larger transcript lives only in the conversation's sandbox. - tools: the app's own tool

head: The proxy
text: agents.proxy is a fetch handler (Request → Response). Serve it at proxyUrl and every path below it (<proxyUrl>/<name>). It checks the job token, adds the user's real token, and sends the request to the MCP server; for the app's own tools, it calls the tool's run. It refuses a job token after the job ends. Do not put the app's session check in front of it. Each of its MCP answers has the header x-byoa-proxy: 1. It is also the relay of a job with plan: 'opencode-go', at <proxyUrl>/_plan/opencode-go/anthropic/v1/… and …/openai/v1/…: it checks the job token (of a job with that plan), adds the user's key, and streams the request to https://opencode.ai/inference/go/… and the answer back, with only the harness's own headers (its user agent, session id, API version and betas; it adds x-opencode-session when there is none). It sends on no other header, so a header that the app's own gateway adds stays behind, and no other path. OpenCode's 401 makes the key expired, its 403 "OpenCode Go subscription required" no-plan. On its 429, the relay asks OpenCode's usage meter (/v1/usage, with the user's key) whether a limit is used up; if so, the job's error is usage-limit with that limit's resetsAt, and byoa keeps it (usageLimit); else it is rate-limited.

head: run(user, options): Job
text: - conversation: the job continues the harness's own session of the jobs before it with the same id, so the agent has their messages. The conversation has its own kept sandbox (the id is its sandboxKey; give no other one), and its job folder stays from job to job: byoa replaces only its own files there (the skills, AGENTS.md, the MCP config, the task). Claude Code: the first job gets --session-id <a new UUID>, the next ones --resume <id>. Codex: the first job starts a thread that is not ephemeral, which its app server names in thread/started; the next ones thread/resume it. Grok: session/new names the session; the next jobs session/resume it. Jobs of one conversation run one at a time, in the order they came. After each job byoa keeps the session id and, up to transcriptBytes, a copy of the session's files, encrypted in the store; when the provider lost the sandbox, the next job writes them into its new one (Claude Code and Grok keep sessions by the job folder's path, which is the same at one provider; Codex by date). When there is no copy, the job starts the conversation again and says so in an error with code conversation. With sandboxPer: 'job', each job of a conversation has a new sandbox and a new job folder, and resumes only from the stored copy. Not with session(). - send (steering): byoa runs each harness under a small driver script (node .byoa/driver.mjs in the job folder) that speaks the CLI's own protocol and gives it each message: Claude Code's stream-json input, C

head: Events (one schema for every harness)
text: run does not throw for job failures: it yields error events and then exactly one end. signed-out / expired: ask the user to sign in again, or for a new key with plan: 'opencode-go' (loginState says the same). no-plan: the key's workspace has no OpenCode Go plan. usage-limit: the user's plan is used up (a 5-hour, weekly, monthly or other limit, or a spend cap); resetsAt (ms since 1970) is when it resets, when the tool said (Claude Code and Codex say it, and for OpenCode Go byoa asks OpenCode's usage meter; Grok Build does not), and usageLimit says the same until then; byoa reads each CLI's own code (Claude Code's api_error, Codex's codexErrorInfo, Grok Build's error_kind), and its words only when that is missing. rate-limited: the lab refused for now (too many requests, or overloaded); byoa keeps nothing. mcp: a server is not connected, its grant failed, it did not answer through the proxy, or the sandbox cannot reach the proxy (then the job did not start). conversation: the conversation's history is gone (the provider lost its sandbox, and its transcript was larger than transcriptBytes); the job runs, as the first of a new session. In start, resumed is true when the harness continued an earlier session of the conversation.

head: listModels(user, h | 'opencode-go'): Promise<ModelInfo[]>
text: The models the user's plan can use with h, as the unmodified CLI lists them with the user's login (Claude Code: its initialize answer; Codex: its app server's model/list; Grok: the initialize answer of grok agent stdio), in a new sandbox that is destroyed after. ModelInfo: { id, name, description, isDefault, efforts, resolved? }; id is what model takes, efforts what effort takes, resolved (Claude Code) the full model name of an alias. Each call starts a sandbox, so keep the list for a while. A Claude Code list waits for the user's running Claude Code jobs. Throws LoginError when h is not signed in. With h 'opencode-go': the plan's chat models, from https://opencode.ai/inference/go/v1/models with the user's key, in the backend (no sandbox). The free models are left out: OpenCode serves them only to its own client. efforts are the model's own, as OpenCode lists them; Claude Code's --effort takes low to max. isDefault is false for each: a job names its model. Throws LoginError when the user has no key.

head: session(user, { harness, setup?, plugins?, mcp?, sandboxKey?, access?, model?, effort?, onWait?, plan? }): Promise<Session>
text: For an app that runs its own program around the unmodified harness. It also takes plan, as run does; args then has the plan's flags. Throws LoginError when the harness is not signed in (or the user has no key of the plan), and ProxyError when the sandbox cannot reach the proxy. The app starts the harness itself, so access changes only the files byoa writes (Codex's MCP config). Session: sandbox, work (the job folder with byoa's files), harness, bin (the pinned binary), version, args (the harness flags for the job's model and effort, for the app's own command line), env (login folder, BYOA_JOB_TOKEN, and for Claude Code MCP_TIMEOUT; with a plan, the plan's settings above), token, mcp ([{ name, url }] at the proxy), missing (servers not connected), failing ([{ name, message }]: servers that did not answer through the proxy), reportLogin('signed-in' 'expired'), close().

head: jobToken(user, { mcp?, ttlMs? }): Promise<JobToken>
text: A job token with no sandbox, for a harness outside byoa's sandboxes (such as on the user's own computer). { token, job, mcp, missing, close() }. Send token as Authorization: Bearer to each mcp[].url.

head: Store adapter
text: The version must change on every write, and a key that is deleted and written again must never get an earlier version back. The one refresh owner of each grant depends on cas. - Postgres: run POSTGRES_SCHEMA once (or postgresSchema('my_table')), then postgresStore({ query: (sql, args) => pool.query(sql, args) }). - Convex: convex/schema.ts has byoa: convexTable(); convex/byoa.ts has export const { get, put, remove, cas } = convexFunctions(); in an action or HTTP action, store: convexStore(ctx, internal.byoa). Call byoa only from actions and HTTP actions, and serve agents.proxy from an HTTP action. - Tests: memoryStore() from @madeyexz/byoa.

head: Sandbox adapter
text: - keep: true: a sandbox byoa keeps for the user. When it times out, the provider pauses it instead of deleting it. - run: a command that exits with a non-zero code resolves; one that runs out of its timeoutMs resolves with exit code 137. - readFile: byoa reads the user's login files and a conversation's transcript with it. Without it, byoa reads a file as base64 on a command's stdout, which a provider may keep in its command history. E2B, Daytona, Instabox, Sprites and the local provider have it. - setTimeout: byoa calls it when a job has the user's AI login, so the time the job waited in line for the login does not count. E2B and Sprites have it, and Daytona for a sandbox of one job. Without it, a job that waited long for the login can reach the sandbox's time before its own ends. - An adapter of the app's own can check itself with the conformance check in byoa's tests (test/helpers/conformance.ts). - E2B: pause ends the sandbox's processes, then takes a full snapshot, with the memory: the next job's resume takes about 0.3 seconds, and node and the harness start warm. When E2B refuses it, because it still saves the sandbox's previous snapshot, byoa takes a snapshot of the files only; the next resume then boots the sandbox again and reads its disk cold, which can add 10 to 20 seconds. E2B keeps a paused sandbox with no time limit, and charges no compute for it. - E2B: the default template is byoa; build it once per pin change with buildE2BTemplate(). Any template with Node 20

head: The fake harness
text: harness: 'fake' runs no model and needs no login. It reads the same MCP config Claude Code would. Each task line call <server>.<tool> <json arguments> is one MCP call through the real proxy; it shows the task's first line as one text event and skips the other lines. The last call's output is the end event's result. In a conversation it keeps each task in a session file and says, in a text event, how many earlier messages it remembers (fake harness remembers 1 earlier messages: <first line>), so an app tests its conversations with no model. Use it with localSandbox() and memoryStore() (or the app's own store) in tests.
